extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and human-rights organizations
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of legal, regulatory, institutional, economic, and social mechanisms that enable or constrain censorship in Ecuador, with examples and reported impacts on media and online expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic Law on Communications (2013) — recognized rights and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecuador’s Organic Law on Communications (passed June 2013) recognizes a right to communication while imposing obligations on media entities (e.g., requirements to collect and store user information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law is described as both recognizing a communication right and imposing burdens on media companies; human-rights groups fear its vague wording, arbitrary sanctions, and threat of civil and criminal penalties may stifle critical voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of 'media lynching' and scope of the prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The law prohibits 'media lynching', a term that appears to extend to any accusation of corruption or investigation of a public official—even those supported with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the term is broad/vague, it can be used to limit reporting on public officials; the page cites concern that this effectively curtails investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website 'ultimate responsibility' for hosted content (including third-party content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites are held to 'ultimate responsibility' for all content they host, including content authored by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision creates strong legal exposure for platforms and may incentivize preemptive removal or moderation of third-party content to avoid sanctions or liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on non-degreed journalists publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The law bans non-degreed journalists from publishing, which effectively outlaws much investigative reporting and citizen journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction narrows who can lawfully publish, undermining informal and grassroots reporting and likely chilling non-professional contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator powers — SUPERCOM and CORDICOM's vague content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The government created SUPERCOM and CORDICOM, regulators that 'imposed a range of vaguely worded content restrictions' and have issued numerous sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SUPERCOM reportedly issued sanctions in more than 300 cases and has punished outlets for not disseminating government 'accomplishments', not using government titles, or not publishing in enforced formats — illustrating how regulatory power can be used to enforce conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online defamation and use of copyright to censor
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard defamation laws apply to online content; there are alleged instances of censorship via overly broad application of copyright law to content critical of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawsuits have been filed against digital news sites for comments critical of the government; these legal routes (defamation/copyright) are used as instruments to suppress critical speech online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cybercafé user registration and surveillance requirements (SENATEL)
rubrics_metrics.description: To use cybercafé services, SENATEL requires registration capturing full name, phone number, passport number, voting certificate number, email address, and home address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive identity collection can deter anonymous speech and facilitate state monitoring of online activity, contributing to chilling effects on online expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2014 constitutional amendment classifying communication as a 'public service'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2014 amendment regarded communication in Ecuador as a 'public service', potentially allowing greater government involvement in media dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reclassifying communication as a public service can expand regulatory justification for government oversight and intervention in what is disseminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISP disclosure obligations under 2012 telecommunications regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2012 telecommunications regulation requires ISPs to fulfill all information requests from the superintendent of telecommunications, allowing access to client addresses and information without a judicial order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lowers legal barriers to obtaining user data from providers, increasing the state's ability to identify and potentially sanction speakers without prior judicial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship and chilling effects resulting from government actions
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile government investigations and public warnings (e.g., president calling for investigation of critical Twitter users) have led to self-censorship and the disabling of comments sections on news sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: La Hora and El Comercio suspended or disabled readers’ comments after government pressure; presidential warnings that protests would be treated as attempts to destabilize the government discouraged protest organization — illustrating indirect censorship through intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and ownership pressures on media outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal restrictions on advertising placement and advertiser fear of reprisals reduce ad revenues for independent outlets; government or state-friendly entities acquiring stakes in media (e.g., 49% stake in El Tiempo) affect editorial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic levers (advertising regulation, market pressure, and ownership changes) are used to limit independent reporting and incentivize pro-government coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting and potential dissolution of NGOs involved in media monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has moved to dissolve NGOs (e.g., Fundamedios in 2015) alleging they acted as 'political actors' rather than impartial observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government proceedings against NGOs that monitor media can chill civil-society oversight and reduce watchdog capacity; the cited case was later reversed but demonstrates a regulatory threat to NGO activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: International press and internet-freedom assessments as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: International organizations classify Ecuador’s press status (Freedom House: 'not free' in 2016; Reporters Without Borders: 'noticeable problems' and rank 109/180) and internet freedom (Freedom on the Net: 'partly free' in 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assessments synthesize legal, regulatory, and practical indicators to evaluate the state of media and internet freedom; they are used as external measures of censorship and restrictions.
